background.definition: Aspergillosis refers to illness due to allergy to, colonization by, or tissue invasion by a species of Aspergillus. Types of aspergillosis include invasive aspergillosis, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis, and saphrophytic disease.

list.listitem: 5.8% incidence of invasive aspergillosis, or 58 new cases per 1000, in intensive care unit (ICU) patients.
1% to 8% incidence in solid organ transplant patients, with highest risk in recipients of lung transplants.
6% to 11% incidence in those receiving a hematopoietic stem cell transplant (less common in autologous transplants [~1%-2%]).
Aspergillus is the most common opportunistic invasive mycosis in the immunocompromised patient.
Aspergillus is a type of mold. Spores (conidia) are frequently inhaled; organisms are widespread in the environment as ubiquitous molds.
Clinical manifestations depend on the host’s immune response: acute hypersensitivity reaction versus chronic allergy (sinusitis) versus invasive disease.
Disease can also be acquired via direct inoculation during procedures, as a result of trauma, or via intravenous drug abuse.
SARS CoV-2 causes damage to the respiratory epithelium, enabling aspergillus invasion in COVID-19 infection.
Aspergillus is a mold; spores (conidia) are inhaled from the environment, and alveolar macrophages serve as the first line of defense.
In a normal host, macrophages will kill the conidia. If there is macrophage dysfunction or a decreased number of macrophages, the conidia are able to germinate and form hyphae.
Hyphae formation should attract neutrophils, if present, which attack the fungus via various mycotoxins and complement inhibitors.
The histopathologic hallmark of aspergillosis is progression of disease across tissue planes.

list.listitem: Suspect aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients who do not respond to antibiotics; invasive pulmonary aspergillosis typically presents with respiratory symptoms, infiltrates, and fever. C
Isolation of Aspergillus via culture or histopathology from a respiratory specimen or tissue sample is the reference standard diagnostic test, but results can take days or weeks. C
Galactomannan antigen detection via ELISA is sensitive and specific, and can be used for early diagnosis and monitoring of therapeutic response. C
The beta-D-glucan (BDG) assay is extremely sensitive for invasive fungal infections and has good negative predictive value, but is not specific for aspergillosis. C

list.listitem: Suspect aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients who do not respond to usual antibiotic therapy.
Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis: Patients typically have cough, dyspnea, fever, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis. Fever is unresponsive to broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Chronic allergic sinusitis related to aspergillosis: Patients usually have headache, congestion, fever; proptosis and cranial nerve palsies can be seen in advanced disease, similar to mucormycoses or zygomycoses.
Disseminated aspergillosis: Patients have fever and sepsis; accompanied by invasion of (most commonly) the liver, spleen, kidney, central nervous system.
Aspergillus tracheobronchitis: Dyspnea, wheezing, cough, can produce mucous plugs; chest x-ray is often unremarkable.
Endocarditis: There is usually fever and signs and symptoms of embolic disease.
Cutaneous involvement of aspergillosis may have rapidly evolving lesions from papules to ulcers. Ulcers enlarge at a rate proportional to the degree of immunosuppression.

Tissue diagnosis with histopathology and culture is considered the reference standard test and is most specific. It does take time, though: Aspergillus appears within 1 to 3 days of culture, but full results can take up to 4 weeks. False negative results are common, especially in patients treated empirically. In general, culture has fairly low sensitivity.

Serum galactomannan ELISA assay identifies a constituent of Aspergillus cell walls. It is used for early detection of infection and to follow response. It has lower sensitivity in ICU patients and solid organ transplant patients; it is more sensitive and specific when used with urine, BAL, or CSF. False positive results are seen with certain antibiotics, and it cross reacts with histoplasma and penicillium species.
PCR for serum galactomannan is highly sensitive and specific, but is is not available in all settings.

The BDG assay is a colorimetric assay that detects another cell well component, but is not specific to Aspergillus. It is highly sensitive with nearly 100% negative predictive value in ruling out invasive fungal infection, but is relatively nonspecific when positive.

Invasive pulmonary aspergerillosis: Pulmonary infiltrates may be seen on on imaging. Nodules, cavitations, or patchy infiltrates are seen on chest x-ray. Chest CT may reveal presence of a halo sign and/or a crescent sign. Among patients with invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, less than 10% of chest x-rays are normal, and less than 3% of chest CTs are normal. In critically ill patients, radiologic signs are often absent.
Aspergillus tracheobronchitis: Chest x-ray is often unremarkable.
Aspergillosis endocarditis: Blood cultures are rarely positive.
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis: sensitization to aspergillus antigens and radiographic findings compatible with the diagnosis. Non-specific findings include eosinophilia.
See for diagnostic criteria.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to evaluation.
See for specific treatment recommendations for different clinical situations.
Voriconazole is the initial treatment of choice for invasive aspergillosis; posaconazole and isavuconazole are alternatives.29, 30 A
Salvage therapies include echinocandins or a combination of 2 drugs, but more studies should be done to evaluate these options. C
Reversal of immunosuppression should be attempted whenever feasible. C
Reversing or halting immunosuppression in affected patients should be the first step in treatment, whenever possible.

Voriconazole or isavuconazole are recommended by guidelines as first line therapy. Voriconazole is given orally and is 100% absorbed in the GI tract. but an IV loading dose should be used for critically ill patients. It has immunomodulatory properties that have been shown to enhance its response to Aspergillus fumigatus.
A trial randomized 527 patients with invasive disease caused by mold including aspergillosis to isavuconazole or voriconazole and found no difference in 42 day mortality (19% vs 20%).

A study randomized 575 persons with invasive aspergillosis to voriconazole 6 mg/kg IV or 300 mg orally bid on day 1 followed by 4 mg/kg IV or 200 mg bid for 12 weeks, or to posaconazole IV or orally 300 mg bid followed by 300 mg once daily for 12 weeks. Posaconazole was non-inferior with regards to 42 day mortality (19% in both groups in the ITT population with proven or probable invasive aspergillosis).

An international randomized controlled trial of 454 patients with hematologic malignancies or hematopoietic stem cell transplants and invasive aspergillosis compared combination therapy with voriconazole plus anidulafungin to voriconazole monotherapy. The trial showed a trend toward decreased mortality at 6 weeks favoring combination therapy (19.3% vs. 27.5%; p = 0.087) and no differences in side effects, including hepatotoxicity.

Amphotericin B is effective, but there has been a high incidence of infusion-related reactions and nephrotoxicity (less common with lipid formulations). A clinical trial comparing voriconazole with amphotericin B found no important differences in cure rates, mortality, or other important outcomes.
Itraconazole is not recommended as first-line therapy but is an option for patients with chornic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis; one trial found stabilization or improvement in 71% of patients.
Echinocandins are not recommended as first line therapy but are an alternative for patients who have failed or cannot tolerate other antifungals.
Treatment duration is for 6 to 12 weeks, or until immune reconstitution and lesions have resolved radiologically.

A randomized trial compared itraconazole 200 mg twice daily with itraconazole in 131 patients with acute allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis that was a complication of asthma. The time to first exacerbation and the number of exacerbations at 2 years of follow-up was similar between groups, as was lung function. "Response" as measured to decline in IgE was greater in the prednisolone group, but so were adverse effects.
See for a summary of specific treatment recommendations.
Surgical resection of aspergilloma may be considered in patients with severe or life-threatening hemoptysis.
Surgical resection is also indicated in those with aspergillus endocarditis, cerebral/optic lesions, osteomyelitis, invasive sinus lesions, skin infection, or empyema.
Invasive aspergillosis is associated with a high mortality rate (up to 80%), especially in transplant (both solid organ and hematopoietic stem cell) patients. B
Even transient colonization with aspergillosis is associated with an increased overall mortality rate in immunocompromised patients. C

Order sputum culture, serum galactomannam (GMA) and serum beta-D-glucan (BDG). Positive sputum or GMA?
Order chest CT. Focal nodule or infiltrate?
Probable aspergillosis. Start voriconazole (amphotericin is alternate).

feature.caption: Criteria for Diagnosis of Invasive Fungal Infection.
feature.feature_body:
Host factors: neutropenia, fever, or graft versus host disease
Microbiologic evidence: positive culture or direct microscopic examination
Minor clinical criteria: cough, chest pain, hemoptysis
Major clinical criteria: computed tomograph with halo sign, air crescent sign, or presence of a cavitary lesion
Data from Hachem R, et al.

feature.caption: Treatment of Aspergillosis.
feature.feature_body:
Presentation of Aspergillosis Treatment of Choice Alternative
Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) Voriconazole 6 mg/kg IV every 12 hours x2, then 4 mg/kg IV every 12 hours until stable. Can switch to 200 mg orally every 12 hours thereafter Options: posaconazole or isavuconazole
Tracheobronchial aspergillosis Same as IPA Same as IPA
Chronic necrotizing pulmonary aspergillosis (CNPA) Same as IPA, but oral triazole (itraconazole or voriconazole) is preferred Same as IPA
Complex aspergilloma Surgical resection IV triazole (same dose as IPA)
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) Oral itraconazole Voriconazole 200 mg orally every 12 hours
Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis (CCPA) Same as CNPA Same as IPA
Empiric treatment for invasive aspergillosis (IA) Same as IPA, use in high risk populations Same as IPA
Prophylaxis for IA (in those with neutropenia, AML, myelodysplastic syndrome) Posaconazole 200 mg orally every 8 hours Itraconazole 200 mg IV every 12 hours x2 doses, then 200 mg/day OR micafungin 50 mg/day IV
Data from Segal BH and Walsh TJ, Vazquez JA, and Oshima K et al.
